name: Nettle root

card.summary: Stinging nettle root extract, studied for prostate symptoms and promoted as an SHBG binder; the testosterone claim rests on lab work.
card.aka: Urtica dioica root, stinging nettle root extract
card.note: Human trials are in benign prostatic hyperplasia, not free-testosterone or appearance outcomes.

quick.overview:
Nettle root is the root of the stinging nettle (Urtica dioica). Extracts are used in European herbal products for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), and in supplement circles it is promoted as a way to bind sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and so leave more testosterone free.

A randomised trial of one root extract in BPH patients reported symptom improvement over placebo. No human trial was found that tests nettle root for testosterone or appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: Laboratory studies have reported that components of nettle root bind SHBG and inhibit its interaction with prostate cell membranes; Grokipedia says that the clinical significance is unclear and unsupported by robust clinical evidence [1]. Lab studies of root extracts also report effects on prostate cell growth and on enzyme activity in prostate tissue [2][3][4].
quick.risks: Grokipedia reports rare mild digestive upset and advises against oral use in pregnancy, and lists possible interactions with diuretics, blood-pressure and diabetes drugs, lithium and warfarin [1]. As an AI-generated source it is unverified.

lead: Nettle root refers to extracts of the roots of Urtica dioica, the common stinging nettle. Root extracts have a long tradition in German phytotherapy for benign prostatic hyperplasia [5].

In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding supplement discussions, nettle root is promoted as an SHBG binder, based on laboratory work showing that certain root constituents bind SHBG [1][6]. Grokipedia states that the clinical significance of this for testosterone is unclear and unsupported by robust clinical evidence [1].

The human evidence that exists concerns urinary symptoms of BPH. A 12-month randomised, placebo-controlled trial of a nettle root extract in 246 patients reported a statistically significant improvement in symptom score compared with placebo [5].
infobox: Sold as a herbal / dietary supplement

paras: SHBG is a blood protein that binds sex hormones. Proponents say that a nettle root compound occupying SHBG leaves more testosterone unbound. Laboratory studies reported that lignans from the root, including one with high affinity, bind human SHBG, and that aqueous root extracts inhibit SHBG binding to prostate membranes [1]. A 2020 biochemical study examined interactions between SHBG and nonsteroidal ligands that enhance androgen activity [6].

Other laboratory studies examined root extracts on prostate cell lines, reporting an antiproliferative effect on LNCaP cancer cells [2], inhibition of enzyme activity in BPH tissue [3] and inhibition of induced prostate growth in mice [4]. A 2024 study tested a combined saw palmetto and nettle root extract on prostate hyperplasia and inflammation in rats and human cells [7].
No studies found that test nettle root for testosterone, free testosterone or appearance outcomes.

For BPH, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial of 459 mg of dry nettle root extract (Bazoton-uno) enrolled 246 patients for one year; the International Prostate Symptom Score fell from 18.7 to 13.0 on the extract versus 18.5 to 13.8 on placebo (p=0.0233) [5]. Grokipedia also cites a systematic review of randomised trials reporting improved symptom scores with Urtica extracts and no significant adverse effects versus controls, without giving its year [1].

Grokipedia reports that oral use is generally considered safe up to a year at recommended doses with rare mild gastrointestinal effects, that oral preparations are contraindicated in pregnancy, and that possible interactions include diuretics, antidiabetic and blood-pressure drugs, lithium and warfarin [1]. These statements are from an AI-generated source and are not independently verified here.

timeline.event: Laboratory study of nettle root extracts on enzyme activity in BPH tissue [3].
Study reports antiproliferative effect of a root extract on LNCaP prostate cancer cells [2].
Report of a 12-month randomised placebo-controlled trial of a root extract in BPH [5].

lore.intro: Nettle root is discussed in supplement circles as a natural way to lower SHBG binding of testosterone; no forum sources were available to quote for this article.

claims.claim: Nettle root binds SHBG and raises free testosterone.
claims.believers: Proponents say that root lignans occupy SHBG, leaving testosterone unbound and available.
claims.experts: In vitro studies report SHBG binding by root components, but Grokipedia states that the clinical significance is unclear and unsupported by robust clinical evidence [1]; no trial of testosterone outcomes was found.
